content: Morphine should generally be prescribed at community health centers (CHCs) unless there is a significant and unavoidable risk of diversion of controlled substances from these facilities. Physicians who manage patients with moderate to severe pain or terminal dyspnea must be adequately trained and legally authorized to prescribe oral and injectable morphine in any dose necessary to provide sufficient relief, as determined by the patient’s needs. Physicians inexperienced in prescribing morphine can be trained using the basic palliative care curriculum outlined in this document or similar curricula. Additionally, doctors should be able to prescribe an adequate supply of morphine to minimize the need for families to make frequent, costly, or burdensome trips for refills. Whenever clinically appropriate, oral morphine should be preferred over its injectable form. All physicians should be trained to assess and manage opioid-related side effects and to avoid inappropriate use of morphine for mild pain or chronic non-malignant pain. In some countries, specially trained nurses may safely and effectively administer opioid therapy. Palliative care and symptom relief should also be integrated into pediatric care, with specific interventions, medicines, equipment, human resources, and social supports tailored to the needs of children. Essential medicines for palliative care include oral and injectable forms of drugs such as amitriptyline, bisacodyl, dexamethasone, diazepam, diphenhydramine, fluconazole, fluoxetine (or other SSRIs), furosemide, haloperidol, hyoscine butylbromide, ibuprofen, lactulose, loperamide, metoclopramide, metronidazole, and morphine. Naloxone, omeprazole, ondansetron, and paracetamol are also critical. In settings where plastic bags are prohibited for environmental reasons, exceptions should be made for medical use. Human resources for palliative care should include trained doctors, nurses, social workers, psychologists, and community health workers (CHWs). These professionals should be equipped to prevent and relieve physical, psychological, social, and spiritual suffering. Physicians trained in basic palliative care should be capable of prescribing opioids like morphine and managing uncomplicated anxiety, depression, or delirium. Nurses and CHWs can provide culturally appropriate psychotherapy and bereavement support, while midwives can play a crucial role in neonatal palliative care and emotional support for parents. This support may include food packages, cash payments, transportation vouchers, and in-kind assistance like blankets and toiletries. Funeral costs should also be covered for families in need, as the inability to provide a culturally appropriate burial can lead to long-term emotional distress. For dying patients, palliative care should focus on comfort-oriented treatment to prevent and relieve suffering while maximizing quality of life. This care should be provided in a quiet, private setting with family presence. Pain and other symptoms must be aggressively managed, and psychological first aid should be available to patients and families. Physicians should be prepared to provide non-specialized psychological care, including prescribing psychotropic medications for uncomplicated mental health conditions. Neonates and critically ill infants are particularly vulnerable and should receive integrated palliative and critical care to maximize comfort and support for their families. Palliative care should be initiated immediately for children with life-limiting abnormalities or malformations, and bereavement support should be accessible after stillbirths or neonatal deaths. Midwives and traditional birth attendants can provide emotional support and guidance to parents during these difficult times. Efforts to integrate palliative care into healthcare systems should follow a public health strategy, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). National policies should mandate access to palliative care and pain control for all, including children. Palliative care services should be integrated into all levels of the healthcare system, starting with cancer centers and expanding to hospitals, CHCs, and home care settings.
